title: Marking: Letting Gemini Do the Heavy Lifting
author: Francesco Rocchi Source: francescorocchi1.substack.com
summary: A language teacher describes his first classroom experiment using Gemini for written essay feedback, framing the tool as a practical solution to the mismatch between how often students should practice extended writing and how often a teacher can provide meaningful marking. He designed two variants: for seniors (Grade 12), Gemini generates a three-column table (original sentence | error explanation | revised sentence) and students hand-copy the result and summarize each critique in their own words — adding friction to prevent passive processing. For juniors (Grade 11), the rewriting column is omitted so students must repair the writing themselves. He honestly names the failure modes: hasty passive processing, student discouragement from the volume of corrections, AI variation across runs of the same prompt, and one observed hallucination. The underlying pedagogical principle: Gemini is not good at assessing in absolute terms but is useful for review and guidance — and grading remains entirely the teacher's responsibility.
points: The fundamental constraint isn't AI capability but teacher marking bandwidth — Gemini allows students to receive feedback on extended writing practice far more frequently than a teacher could manually provide it.

The two-variant design applies cognitive load reasoning: seniors get the model rewriting (they need the example first), while juniors omit it to force productive effort in generating their own corrections.

Hand-copying the corrected version and summarizing each critique in the student's own words are deliberate friction mechanisms to prevent the AI's fluency from substituting for the student's engagement — 'the danger is that the work might be done hastily and passively, passing through the students' heads like water through a sieve.'

Known failure modes: passive processing, student discouragement from heavy correction volume, variation across runs of the same prompt (the AI's probabilistic nature), and occasional hallucination — the author observed one character substituted for another.

Gemini is not an evaluator — it is a review-and-guidance tool; the teacher retains full responsibility for grading and must monitor carefully before drawing conclusions about whether learning outcomes actually improve.
quotes: Gemini is not good at measuring and assessing (at least in absolute terms), but is good at reviewing and offering guidance, or so it seems.

As homework, my students won't just have to use the AI; they also have to hand-copy the corrected result into their notebooks and summarize, in their own words, the critiques the AI made. The point of this is to have proof that the work was done and, through the act of copying and summarizing the critique, to force them to carefully read not just the revised version, but the corrections themselves.
The danger is that the work might be done hastily and passively, passing through the students' heads like water through a sieve. I'll have to monitor that.
If you give the same prompt and the same essay to the AI, the results can change slightly — which is obvious, given that these texts are generated probabilistically every time.
None of this has anything to do with assigning a final grade, which remains my responsibility.
